title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what is over, what was aimed at, what was expected

questions.prompt: Complete this line from the yearly report of an association in Kairouan. Only the sentence itself tells you which form to choose: "Last winter the volunteers moved the evening class to Saturday morning so that the pupils from the villages ___ the last bus home."

options.text: can catch
will catch
would have caught
could catch

questions.explanation: "could catch" is the form: a clause of purpose carries a modal, and that modal follows the tense of the main verb — can and will after a present, a present perfect or a future, could and would after a past. The main verb here is moved, and Last winter closes the question, so the past side is the only one open. "can catch" is the present member of the pair, and it leaves the sentence with a past main verb and a present purpose, which no English sentence does. "will catch" makes the same clash with the future; its own past partner, would catch, would in fact have been correct here, and it is not among the four. And "would have caught" adds a perfect that says the bus was expected to be caught and was not; a purpose clause tells what was wanted at the time of the action, and it never reports afterwards whether it worked.

questions.prompt: An editor is shortening the lines of a school magazine before it goes to the printer. She has this one in front of her: "Rania takes the six o'clock bus so that she can be at the workshop before eight." She wants a shorter line that says exactly the same thing. Which line does she print?

options.text: Rania takes the six o'clock bus to be at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus for being at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus so to be at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus, so she is at the workshop before eight.

questions.explanation: "Rania takes the six o'clock bus to be at the workshop before eight." is the shorter line: the two halves of the original have the same subject, Rania takes and she can be, and when the person is the same the clause is not needed at all — an infinitive of purpose carries the aim on its own, and it attaches to the subject already there. "Rania takes the six o'clock bus for being at the workshop before eight." copies your own language, which puts a preposition and a verbal noun in front of an aim; English gives an aim with to and the base verb. "Rania takes the six o'clock bus so to be at the workshop before eight." keeps half of so that and drops the half that matters: so that must be followed by a subject and a verb, and so on its own is never followed by an infinitive. And "Rania takes the six o'clock bus, so she is at the workshop before eight." is correct English but has changed the message: it now reports what happens every morning instead of what she is aiming at, and the editor was told to keep the meaning.

questions.prompt: Khaled started work at a bakery in Bizerte in June, and the first weeks were hard: he had never in his life got out of bed before dawn. It is now September, and the four o'clock alarm costs him nothing at all. Which sentence does he say about himself today?

options.text: I used to get up at four.
I am used to get up at four.
I am used to getting up at four.
I am not used to getting up at four.

questions.explanation: "I am used to getting up at four." says what September has changed: be used to means that something has stopped feeling strange, it takes a noun or an -ing form after it, and it is true of him now. "I used to get up at four." is the other structure altogether, three fixed words plus a base verb, and it puts the four o'clock mornings in the past — but he is still at the bakery, and the question asks what he says about himself today. "I am used to get up at four." starts on the right structure and then puts a base verb where the -ing form belongs; after the to of be used to, English never uses an infinitive. And "I am not used to getting up at four." is built correctly and says the opposite of the situation: it is what he could have said in June, not what he says once the alarm costs him nothing.

questions.prompt: At the end of a long meeting, the manager of a small printing works in Sousse says, to nobody in particular: "I should have taken on a second apprentice in January." One of these four statements is what her sentence tells you about last January. Which one?

options.text: She took on a second apprentice, and the workshop is better for it.
She did not take on a second apprentice, and she thinks that was wrong.
She took on a second apprentice, and she thinks that was wrong.
She has not yet decided whether to take on a second apprentice this year.

questions.explanation: "She did not take on a second apprentice, and she thinks that was wrong." is what the sentence tells you: should have plus the past participle names something sensible that was not carried out, and it adds the judgement that it ought to have been; and since she is speaking about herself, that judgement is a regret. "She took on a second apprentice, and the workshop is better for it." turns the facts round, because should have never describes an action that was performed, and it lends her a satisfaction her words do not contain. "She took on a second apprentice, and she thinks that was wrong." is what shouldn't have taken on would have said: the negative is the form that reports a thing done and regretted, and the positive is the form that reports a thing left undone. And "She has not yet decided whether to take on a second apprentice this year." leaves the matter open, when should have closes it: January is behind her, and the choice can no longer be made.

questions.prompt: A carpenter in Nabeul varnished a door at half past two, and the tin says that this varnish is dry in ninety minutes. He is in the office with his back to the workshop, the clock over the door says four, and he says to the apprentice sitting next to him: "That door should have dried." What is he doing with those words?

options.text: He is blaming the apprentice for using too much varnish.
He is saying what he expects to be true at this moment.
He is regretting the moment he chose to varnish the door.
He is telling the apprentice to carry the door outside.

questions.explanation: "He is saying what he expects to be true at this moment." is what the sentence does: should have carries a second value, far from regret, an assumption about what has probably happened already, and he is doing arithmetic — half past two plus ninety minutes, against a clock that says four. His back is turned: he has seen nothing, and he has worked it out. "He is blaming the apprentice for using too much varnish." reads a reproach into a calculation, and a reproach needs somebody who failed to do what was expected, which nobody here has. "He is regretting the moment he chose to varnish the door." hears the value the structure carries most often, but a regret judges a choice and calls it wrong, and he calls nothing wrong. And "He is telling the apprentice to carry the door outside." turns a remark into an instruction; should have plus a past participle either looks back or works something out, and it never gives an order.

questions.prompt: A youth centre in Gafsa pins up this notice. "ASSISTANT LIBRARIAN, six months, part-time. The work: shelving, lending, and helping pupils find what they need. Who may apply: candidates who hold a two-year degree in documentation AND have done at least one internship in a library. Training: two weeks, paid, before you start. Applications close on 30 April." Four young people from the town read it on the same afternoon. Which one may apply?

options.text: Hichem, who has a two-year degree in documentation and has never set foot in a library except as a reader.
Sonia, who has done two internships in a library and left university after her first year.
Rania, who has a two-year degree in documentation and did a month's internship in a library last year.
Mehdi, who has a two-year degree in documentation, one internship, and posted his letter on 2 May.

questions.explanation: "Rania, who has a two-year degree in documentation and did a month's internship in a library last year." is the only one who may apply: the notice joins its two conditions with AND, so both have to be met, and she is the one who holds the degree and has served the internship, in time. "Hichem, who has a two-year degree in documentation and has never set foot in a library except as a reader." meets the first condition and fails the second, and with AND one condition out of two is nothing. "Sonia, who has done two internships in a library and left university after her first year." fails the other way round: two internships do not replace the qualification the notice asks for, and one year is not the two-year degree. And "Mehdi, who has a two-year degree in documentation, one internship, and posted his letter on 2 May." meets both conditions and still cannot be considered, because the notice closes on 30 April; a date at the bottom of an advertisement is a condition like the others.
